title: Dhruva's mantra
hookLine: a little prince is pulled off his father's lap, and walks into the forest with one mantra
carry: sadhana is the practice you keep returning to

lines: A BOY WALKS INTO THE FOREST.
cards: A little prince named Dhruva climbs onto his father's lap. His stepmother, the king's favorite queen, pulls him off.
Only her own son belongs there, she says; if Dhruva wants that seat, he should pray to the Lord to be born again as her son. The king says nothing. Dhruva runs to his own mother, Suniti, in tears.
She tells him the only one who can truly help is the Lord, Vishnu. So the boy walks out toward the forest. The Bhagavata Purana tells it, and Hindu children still hear it.

teach.b: On the way, the sage Narada meets him and tries to turn him back: you're only a child, this is too hard. Dhruva won't go home.

teach.h: DAY AFTER DAY, IN THE FOREST.
teach.b: So Narada gives him what a teacher gives: a place, the forest of Madhuvana by the Yamuna, and a mantra. Om namo bhagavate vasudevaya: I bow to the Lord. Dhruva repeats it day after day.

In the telling he eats less and less, fruit, then leaves, then only water, then air, until his practice weighs on the whole universe, and Vishnu comes to stand in front of him. And here's the turn the story is loved for.
The boy had come for a throne.

teach.h: SORRY HE ASKED FOR SO LITTLE.
teach.b: Vishnu grants it, but on the walk home, having seen the Lord, Dhruva is sorry, the story says, that he asked for so small a thing.
He does rule, later, and at the end he's given a place in the sky that never moves: the pole star, still called Dhruva.

teach.h: THE PRACTICE YOU KEEP RETURNING TO.
teach.b: The tradition's word for what he did is sadhana: a spiritual practice kept up until it becomes yours.
Very often it's japa, a mantra from a teacher or the family, repeated on a mala of a hundred and eight beads, every day.
The Yoga Sutra says what makes practice hold, in paraphrase: a long time, without breaks, and with care. Most of us won't live on air in a forest.
But the same fingers coming back to the same beads is Dhruva's road, sized for a life.

how: Many Hindus keep a daily sadhana, often japa: a mantra from a teacher or the family, repeated on a mala of 108 beads at about the same time each day. Dhruva's story is told to children as a picture of steady devotion.

o: a teacher's blessing given at initiation
a single long retreat done once in a lifetime
a spiritual practice kept up until it becomes yours

p: the boy who wouldn't go home
the sage who gave him a mantra

s: a practice only counts if it's long and hard
the Yoga Sutra says long, unbroken, and with care. it doesn't say hard or perfect.
when Vishnu appeared, Dhruva was sorry he'd come asking for a throne
in the Bhagavata, seeing the Lord made the throne a small thing to have asked for.
sadhana is a practice you finish once and move on from
it's kept up, day after day, until it becomes yours.

games.q: you want one practice to last all summer. what do Dhruva's story and the Yoga Sutra point to?
o: one huge effort the first week, then a rest.
one mantra, every day, kept with care.
a new practice whenever the old one gets boring.
games.why: dhruva kept one mantra, day after day, until the Lord came. the Yoga Sutra says practice holds when kept long, unbroken, and with care. that's sadhana.

practice: If you have a mala, hold it in your right hand; if not, count on your fingers. Say a mantra softly, once per bead or finger: Dhruva's, om namo bhagavate vasudevaya, or om namah shivaya, or the name of God your family uses.
If you don't pray, repeat one slow word, like peace. Don't count for a score. When the mind wanders, simply go on to the next bead, the way Dhruva went on to the next day.

wordCard.voice: Sadhana. A spiritual practice kept up until it becomes yours, like the mantra Dhruva repeated in the forest until the Lord came.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: sadhana, a steady spiritual practice, the one you return to.

carryVoice: Your line: sadhana is the practice you keep returning to. Dhruva's star still doesn't move. Tomorrow, how the Gita ends. Until tomorrow.
